---
title: "Exercises — Spatial libraries"
---

Pen and paper. Each problem is a choice you would have to make at the bench, or a symptom you
would have to explain from a data set.

# Part 1 — Getting the RNA onto the array

## E1. Pick a permeabilisation time

A tissue-optimisation slide has four wells. You permeabilise each for a different time,
make fluorescent cDNA on the slide, and image it:

| Time | What the image shows |
|---|---|
| 3 min | Faint, patchy signal, strongest in the least dense regions |
| 6 min | Bright signal, sharp edges, follows the tissue outline |
| 12 min | Brighter overall, edges soft, a halo outside the tissue |
| 24 min | Bright and uniform, tissue shape barely visible |

a. Which time do you choose, and why not the brightest well?
b. What does the 3 min well tell you about *which* RNA is released first?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
What would the signal under one cell look like if RNA spent a long time free before it was
caught?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 6 min. Brightness is not the goal: **localisation** is. Past 6 min the extra signal is
   RNA that has travelled, so each spot reports a blend of its neighbours and the outline of
   the tissue is lost. Choose the shortest time that gives full, sharp signal.
b. Short, abundant, loosely bound transcripts and thin or loose tissue regions come out first.
   A short time therefore gives a biased sample of the transcriptome as well as a weak one,
   which is a second reason to avoid under-permeabilising.
:::

## E2. An archive block

A collaborator offers 12-year-old formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumour blocks and wants a
whole-transcriptome spatial map with Visium-type capture.

a. Name two things formalin fixation and age do to RNA that threaten oligo-dT capture.
b. What kind of capture would you ask for instead, and which property of the RNA does it
   depend on?
c. Why does the same chemistry do no harm in FISSEQ or STARmap, and in fact help?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The RNA is cut into short pieces, and poly(A) tails are lost or crosslinked and
   unavailable, so an oligo-dT oligo has little to catch. Whatever is caught is biased to the
   3' ends that survived.
b. Probe pairs that hybridise to short stretches of RNA, are ligated, and are then captured
   on the array. They depend only on a short stretch of sequence surviving, not on the tail.
c. In situ methods crosslink on purpose: the crosslinks anchor the cDNA or amplicon to the
   cell's protein, so it stays where the RNA was. They also use probes, or primers that bind
   anywhere, so degraded RNA is less of a problem.
:::

# Part 2 — Arrays and resolution

## E3. Resolution against sensitivity

A Visium spot is 55 µm across and yields a median of 5,000 UMIs. You move to 10 µm beads
and assume the same capture density per area.

a. How many UMIs do you expect per bead?
b. A cell is about 10 µm across. About how many Stereo-seq positions (0.5 µm pitch) fall
   inside one cell, and what would you do with them?
c. Why do these numbers argue for judging a run on UMIs per area rather than per spot?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Area ratio (55 / 10)² ≈ 30, so about 5,000 / 30 ≈ 170 UMIs. Real capture density differs
   between methods, so treat this as the expected scale only.
b. (10 / 0.5)² = 400 positions, each with very few UMIs. Individual positions are not
   interpretable, so they are binned (into cell-sized bins or segmented cells).
c. Per-spot UMIs fall with the square of the spot size by construction; the quantity that
   carries over between methods is UMIs per unit area, together with how many UMIs your
   analysis needs per unit of tissue to say something.
:::

## E4. Where the barcode gets its coordinate

For each array, say when and how the coordinate of a barcode becomes known, and name one way
it could go wrong.

a. A printed Visium-type slide
b. A Slide-seq bead pour
c. A Stereo-seq chip

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Known from manufacturing: the position of each barcode is a property of the printed slide.
   Failure: a printing or spotting defect that cannot be recovered afterwards.
b. Found after the beads settle, by sequencing the beads in place. Failure: beads that decode
   badly or overlap are lost, and the density of the pour sets how much is usable.
c. Found before the tissue touches the chip, by sequencing the coordinate identifier of every
   nanoball. Failure: the chip is a fixed investment, and a decoding error is paid for by
   every sample on it.
:::

# Part 3 — Barcoding in tissue and choosing regions

## E5. A missing phosphate

In DBiT-seq the A oligo has a 5' phosphate and the B oligo ends in a 3'-OH, with a splint
holding both beside one nick. A batch of A oligos arrives **without** the 5' phosphate.

a. What happens to the ligation?
b. The PCR primers anneal to the handle on the B oligo. What do you see in the library?
c. How would you tell this apart from a failed reverse transcription?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
What does T4 DNA ligase need on the two sides of a nick?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. T4 DNA ligase needs a 5' phosphate and a 3'-OH at the nick. Without the phosphate the
   nick stays open and B is never joined to A.
b. The handle that PCR needs sits on B, so tagged cDNA that lacks B cannot be captured or
   amplified: a weak or empty library, not a library with half the address.
c. A failed reverse transcription gives little cDNA at all, which shows up when the cDNA is
   first amplified. A missing phosphate gives normal cDNA that is lost only after the B
   ligation. A tube test, ligating the A and B oligos on the splint without tissue, separates
   the two; phosphorylating the A oligos with T4 polynucleotide kinase fixes the batch.
:::

## E6. Channels and barcodes

You want to cover 5 mm × 5 mm of tissue with 20 µm pitch pixels using DBiT-style flows.

a. How many A and B barcodes do you need, and how many pixels is that?
b. If each barcode is 8 nt, how many are available, and what limits how many you can use?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. 5000 / 20 = 250 channels each way: 250 A barcodes, 250 B barcodes, 62,500 pixels.
b. 4⁸ = 65,536 sequences, so there are enough in principle. What limits the usable set is
   that barcodes must differ from each other in several positions, so that a sequencing error
   does not turn one barcode into another. That set is much smaller than 65,536.
:::

## E7. Regions or a grid?

A tumour section has ten glands of interest, each a few hundred cells. You must choose
between GeoMx and a capture array with 55 µm spots.

a. State one reason for each.
b. What does GeoMx give up?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. GeoMx collects all the tags from each gland into one sample, so every region has many
   cells' worth of signal, and probes tolerate formalin-fixed tissue. The grid would give
   you every part of the tissue, including regions you did not anticipate.
b. Everything inside a region is averaged. You cannot ask about structure within it, and
   regions must be chosen before you know what the data would show.
:::

# Part 4 — Reading in place

## E8. Why crosslink the cDNA?

In FISSEQ the cDNA contains aminoallyl-dUTP and is crosslinked to cellular protein before
circularisation. What would the image look like if that step were left out, and what
chemical property makes the step possible?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The cDNA copies are free molecules and would diffuse out of the cell during the many washes
that sequencing needs. Rolonies would be missing or smeared, and the image would not
correspond to the cell it came from. The modified nucleotide carries a primary amine that a
bifunctional amine-reactive crosslinker can tie to protein amines of the cell.
:::

# Self-check

1. Why is imaging done before permeabilisation in a Visium workflow?
2. What is the UMI for in a spatial spot?
3. Name two ways a method can make a coordinate become a sequence.
4. Which methods do not produce a library at all?
5. Why does fixation affect which capture chemistry is possible?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. After permeabilisation and reverse transcription the section no longer looks like the
   tissue; the image must come from the intact section.
2. It counts molecules rather than reads, so PCR duplicates are not mistaken for expression,
   which matters when a spot holds a few hundred molecules.
3. A barcode on a printed, bead or DNB array whose position is known or decoded, or a pair of
   barcodes laid down by perpendicular flows in the tissue.
4. FISSEQ and STARmap: the amplicons are read under a microscope.
5. Poly(A) capture needs intact tails; fixation and age damage them, so probe-based or in
   situ chemistry is needed.
:::
